transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. [Name], I'm here because... well, it's about my apartment building. I've been living there for a while now, and lately, it's just become completely obvious to me what's going on. The people there, the other tenants, they are watching me. I mean, they are keeping track of every single time I leave my apartment, every time I come back, who I might be talking to, where I might be going. It's like they have this schedule of my comings and goings. And it's not just that they're watching, they are actually slipping notes about me to the management office. I see them doing it, or well, I know they're doing it. They leave these papers, these notes, and everybody, my sister, the manager, they all keep telling me, "Oh, it's just regular notices, they're putting them on everyone's doors," but I know that's not true. I know those notes are about me, reporting on what I'm doing. It's just so stressful, you know, constantly feeling eyes on you the minute you step out into the hallway, having to look over your shoulder just to go down to the mailbox. It's just... it's exhausting, and I just needed to talk to someone about it because nobody else seems to understand what's really happening.

Besides feeling stressed and suspicious, have you noticed any changes in your mood lately—like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually energetic, elated, or needing much less sleep than usual?

Well, energetic? No, absolutely not. I mean, I wish I was energetic, but it's actually been quite the opposite for a while now. It's... it's hard to explain without getting into the whole routine of it, but it starts right when I wake up. Most mornings, I wake up and there's just this... this heavy, hollow feeling sitting right in my chest. It's like the day has already gone completely bad before I even get my feet on the floor, you know? And I just lie there, looking at the ceiling, thinking about having to face the hallway, face the building, and it's just so draining. It's not just a passing sadness, it's this deep, sinking weight that just drags me down. I used to be able to get up and at least make a pot of coffee and look out the window, but now, it takes everything I have just to convince myself to get out from under the covers. And it stays with me, too. It's not like I get up and it shakes off. It just hangs around all day, making everything feel so... pointless, I guess. So no, definitely not elated or energetic. Just really, really low and heavy.

Have you noticed whether these feelings of being watched and monitored happen only during the times you're feeling this low and heavy, or do they continue even during periods when your mood feels more normal?

Well, see, that's the thing that really gets to me... because you'd think, wouldn't you, that if it was just me being down in the dumps, it would all just go away when I had a good stretch. But... well, I remember a little while back, there was this spell... it lasted for several weeks, actually. I was actually doing a bit better for a minute there. I wasn't waking up with that awful, hopeless feeling crushing my chest every single morning. I was actually getting out of bed at a decent hour, and I was even eating a bit better. I remember making myself some proper oatmeal on the stove, taking the time to actually cook something instead of just sitting there staring at the wall all day with an empty stomach. 

But the thing is... the neighbors, they didn't stop. Not for a second. Even when I was feeling alright, even when I had a bit of an appetite and the mornings weren't so heavy and dark, I still knew exactly what they were doing out there in the hall. I'd be at the stove, stirring my pot, and I could just feel it. I still knew they were watching my door and reporting on me to the office. It didn't matter one bit that my mood had lifted or that I was eating my meals. The watching, the keeping tabs on me, the reporting... that just kept right on going, same as always. So it's definitely not just when I'm feeling low. They don't take a break just because I'm having a better week, they're always out there.
How long, in total, have you been feeling that your neighbors are watching you and reporting on you to the management—has this been going on for months, or longer?

Well, it's... it's been a long time. It feels like forever, honestly, but if I really stop and think about it, if I trace it back to when I first started noticing the little things—you know, the way the floorboards would creak right outside my door, or how someone always seemed to be checking their mail at the exact same time I was—it's been going on for about a year and a month now. 

I remember because it started right around the time the weather was turning last year, just getting cold. At first, I thought maybe I was just being overly aware, you know? Like, you move into a place, or you've been there a while, and suddenly you just start noticing the patterns of the people around you. But then it became a daily thing. Every single day, for thirteen months. A year and a month of having to listen to every sound in the hallway, of knowing they're out there, keeping their little logs and sliding those notes under the manager's door. It's not something you can just ignore, not when it's been happening day in and day out for over a year. You start to realize it's not just a coincidence, it's a dedicated effort. They've been at it for a year and a month, never missing a beat, just constantly watching.
Aside from believing your neighbors are watching and reporting on you, have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear, or seen things that others didn't see?

No, no, I've never had anything like that. I mean, I know what you're asking—like if I'm hearing things that aren't there, or seeing ghosts or shadows or whatever it is people talk about. But no, it's nothing like that. My ears work just fine, and my eyes work just fine. In fact, sometimes I think they work a little too well, you know? Because I'm picking up on the real things, the actual things happening right outside my door. 

I'm not sitting here having conversations with thin air. When I hear the floorboards creak, it's because someone is actually standing there. It's a heavy, distinct sound—you get to know the sound of a size ten boot on cheap linoleum when you hear it every day for thirteen months. And I don't see things that aren't there, either. I see the blinds twitching across the way. I see the way the neighbor down the hall quickly turns his head and pretends to be fumbling with his keys the second I open my door. It's all real. It's very, very real. 

So no, I don't hear voices whispering in my head or see visions or anything like that. I just see and hear exactly what they're doing, the actual physical things they're doing to keep tabs on me. It's frustrating, honestly, when people think you're just making it up or imagining things, because I'm very grounded in reality. I just happen to be in a reality where the people around me are constantly monitoring my every move, and I'd have to be deaf and blind not to notice it. But as far as hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there? Absolutely not. Never happened.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (neighbors surveilling and reporting on her) persisting for over 13 months, well beyond the 1-month threshold for delusional disorder. Critically, the delusion persisted unchanged even during a period of mood improvement (weeks of better appetite, energy, and mood), demonstrating that the delusional belief is not confined to mood episodes, which argues against a mood disorder with psychotic features. There are no hallucinations, no bizarre delusions, and no other symptoms suggestive of schizophrenia (no disorganized speech, negative symptoms, or hallucinations), and functioning outside the delusional theme appears relatively preserved. This pattern—an isolated, systematized persecutory delusion without hallucinations, thought disorder, or the full schizophrenia symptom complex—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22).
